optionalFindings.note: controlsAfterWait observes only the console. In dual mode the file queue's control retention after the timed-out wait (the output that is actually still pending) is not measured. A separate fileControlsAfterWait gauge (expected 1 for dual, 0 elsewhere) would show directly that the timed-out caller detaches without stripping the file output's registered boundary. This is optional because the per-output Pending and TimedOut result assertions and the eventual-disposition check already cover the observable contract.

No corruption control targets the dual-specific console override (py:59) or dual's controlsAfterWait. A control such as changing the dual console flush to 'Pending', or setting dual controlsAfterWait to 1, would pin the corrected expectation against regression.

qualificationOptionalFindings.text: The task-local initial claude-review.json could not be found. planning/logging/evidence/wp05-s08-t03/claude-review.json does not exist, and no s08-t03 evidence directory exists under planning/logging/evidence. R1/O1/O2/O3 were checked against the descriptions in the request, not against the original finding text. For O2 I could confirm eight new controls (registered, retained, later-facts, eventual, outputs, console-record, later-failure, file-record) but not that they are the same seven checks the initial review asked for.

The C# Validate used by the in-process unit DataRows and the child-process integration test checks less than the Python verifier. It checks heldControls/controlsAfterWait only for cancelled modes (FlushResultExpectations.cs:22). It does not check actual console/file records, eventual diagnostics pending == 0, later-facts exclusion, the later write failure, UTC label parsing or the PID. The Python verifier (verify-flush-results.py:34-35, 65-76) does check these. So those properties are proven only on the native verifier path. Optionally add the same checks to the C# Validate.

The JoiningClock blocks the callback before it enters FlushDeadline.Tick. By the time it is released, DisposeAsync has already set disposed=true, so Tick returns early. The test does prove the general requirement: an active .NET timer callback is joined (await actual.DisposeAsync) before the public task completes and before the source is disposed, since lifetime.Dispose follows sequentially at FlushDeadline.cs:71-72. What it does not exercise is the narrower window where a callback has passed the gate with expire=true and is about to call lifetime.Cancel() outside the gate (FlushDeadline.cs:56) while disposal begins. The code handles that window correctly by inspection, so this is a coverage note, not a defect.
